questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: When I was five, I ____ ride a bicycle.
option_feedback: *may* is for permission or possibility, not ability.
*When I was five* is past: use *could*.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: ____ I borrow your notes, Ma'am?
option_feedback: *Would I borrow* is not a request form.
*Must I ...?* asks about obligation, not permission.
*Shall I* offers to do something; it does not ask permission to borrow.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: After months of practice, she ____ to swim across the river last summer.
questions.explanation: A specific past achievement → *was able to*.
option_feedback: *could* + *to* is wrong; and for one specific achievement we prefer *was able to*.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: I'm sorry, I ____ come to your party tomorrow; I have an exam.
option_feedback: *mustn't* means you are not allowed; this is about being unable.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: Students ____ use calculators in the board exam; they are not allowed.
option_feedback: *might not* is a possibility, not a rule.
*need not* means it is not necessary, not that it is forbidden.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: Next year I ____ drive, because I will be eighteen.
option_feedback: *could* is past or a weak possibility.
*can* cannot show a future ability that depends on something; use *will be able to*.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: Take an umbrella. It ____ rain later.
option_feedback: *must* would mean you are sure it will rain.
Then there would be no need for an umbrella.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: That ____ be Neha at the door; she has gone to Canada.
option_feedback: *may* suggests it is possible, but she is in Canada.
*must* would mean you are sure it is her.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: Everyone is wearing a coat. It ____ be very cold outside.
option_feedback: The evidence shows it is cold, not the opposite.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: I'm not sure where Kabir is. He ____ be in the library, or perhaps in the canteen.
option_feedback: You are not sure, so *must* (certainty) is wrong.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: The road is wet. It ____ rained last night.
option_feedback: *should have* criticises; here we are deducing.
The wet road shows that it did rain.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: He ____ stolen the money; he was with me the whole day.
questions.explanation: Sure something did not happen → *can't have* + V3.
option_feedback: He was with you, so you are sure he did NOT.
*should have* means it was the right thing to do.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: She didn't reply. She ____ seen my message.
questions.explanation: Guess about the past → *might not have* + V3.
option_feedback: *mustn't have* is not used for deduction.
That would criticise her for seeing it.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: All passengers ____ wear seat belts during take-off.
Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: You ____ bring your own lunch; it will be served at the camp.
option_feedback: *can't* means not able or not allowed.
It is not forbidden, just unnecessary.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: Yesterday I ____ stay late at school to finish the project.
option_feedback: *must* has no past form; use *had to*.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: In India we ____ drive on the left side of the road.
option_feedback: Driving on the left is a rule, not a choice.
*would* is for habits or imagined situations.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: Do I ____ fill in this form again?
questions.explanation: *Do I have to ...?* asks about necessity.
option_feedback: *ought* needs *to*, and *Do I ought* is wrong.
*Do I must* is wrong; *must* never follows *do*.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: You ____ have bought vegetables. Mother had already bought them.
option_feedback: *couldn't have bought* means it was impossible.
*mustn't have* is not used here; the buying was simply unnecessary.
*can't have bought* would mean you are sure he did not buy.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: You look pale. You ____ see a doctor.
option_feedback: *would* is not used alone for advice.
*can* only says it is possible; advice needs *should*.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: We ____ to respect our national flag.
option_feedback: *should* takes no *to*; the blank is followed by *to*.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: ____ you please pass me the salt?
option_feedback: *Must you* sounds like a complaint, not a request.
*Should you* is not a polite request form.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: ____ I carry your bag for you, Grandma?
option_feedback: *Need I* asks if it is necessary.
*Must I* asks if it is compulsory.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: You'd ____ leave now or you will miss the train.
option_feedback: *'d should* is not a correct form.
*'d best to* is not a correct form.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: When we were children, we ____ play in the fields every evening.
option_feedback: In positive sentences the form is *used to*.
*must* is not used for past habits.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: ____ you live long and be happy!
Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: ____ you mind closing the door?
questions.explanation: *Would you mind + V-ing?* is a polite request.
option_feedback: *Must you mind* is not a request.
The fixed polite pattern is *Would you mind ...?*

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: I failed the test. I ____ studied harder.
option_feedback: *must have studied* means you are sure you studied.
*can have* is not used this way.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: Why didn't you ask me? I ____ helped you.
option_feedback: *must have helped* means you are sure I helped.
*should helped* is wrong; modal + V1 or *have* + V3.
*can have* is not used for missed chances.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the most suitable modal: He ____ driven so fast. That is why he had an accident.
questions.explanation: Criticism of a past action → *shouldn't have* + V3.
option_feedback: *mustn't have* is not used to criticise past actions.
*can't have* means you are sure he did not drive fast.
*needn't driven* is not a correct form.

Blank (a):

Blank (b):
option_feedback: That would mean phones are optional; a notice like this forbids them.

questions.question:
Read the passage and choose the correct option for the blank.

*Notice: All students (a) ____ report to the auditorium by 9 a.m. Students (b) ____ bring their mobile phones. Those who wish to participate in the quiz (c) ____ register with the class teacher. Parents (d) ____ attend the prize distribution if they wish.*

Blank (c):
option_feedback: *can't register* makes no sense for those who wish to take part.

questions.question:
Read the passage and choose the correct option for the blank.

*Notice: All students (a) ____ report to the auditorium by 9 a.m. Students (b) ____ bring their mobile phones. Those who wish to participate in the quiz (c) ____ register with the class teacher. Parents (d) ____ attend the prize distribution if they wish.*

Blank (d):
option_feedback: *if they wish* shows it is optional.
*ought to* is a duty, but it is optional.
*if they wish* shows it is optional, not compulsory.

questions.question: Identify the error and choose the correct correction: *She can speaks four languages.*
Identify the error and choose the correct correction: *You should to drink more water.*
Identify the error and choose the correct correction: *He musts complete the work by Monday.*
Identify the error and choose the correct correction: *I will can meet you tomorrow.*
options: will can → will be able to
questions.explanation: Two modals cannot be used together.

questions.question: Identify the error and choose the correct correction: *You should have went to the doctor.*
option_feedback: After a modal, *have* never changes to *has*.

questions.question: Identify the error and choose the correct correction: *Does she can swim?*
option_feedback: The question form is the problem, not the modal.

questions.question: Identify the error and choose the correct correction: *We mustn't buy bread; there is plenty at home.*
Identify the error and choose the correct correction: *We ought respect our teachers.*
Identify the error and choose the correct correction: *Yesterday I can't finish my homework.*
option_feedback: The modal must fit the time, not the other way round.

questions.question: Identify the error and choose the correct correction: *He must have forget his keys.*
Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: She can't to be at school; it's a holiday.
She doesn't can be at school; it's a holiday.
She can't be at school; it's a holiday.
She mustn't be at school; it's a holiday.
option_feedback: Certainty that something is not true takes *can't*, not *mustn't*.

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: You could has told me earlier.
You could have told me earlier.
You could have tell me earlier.

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: We used to live in Bhavnagar.
We use to live in Bhavnagar.
We used to lived in Bhavnagar.
We were used to live in Bhavnagar.
option_feedback: *be used to* means *accustomed to* and takes V-ing.

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: I must waited for an hour.
I musted wait for an hour.
I had to waited for an hour.
I had to wait for an hour.

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: Would you like to some tea?

questions.question: What does the modal in bold express? *My grandfather **can** still read without glasses.*
option_feedback: Nobody is allowing anything; it is about what he is able to do.
It is a fact about his ability.

questions.question: What does the modal in bold express? *Don't call now; she **might** be sleeping.*
option_feedback: Sleeping is not a duty here.
It is a guess, not about ability.

questions.question: What does the modal in bold express? *You have walked 20 km. You **must** be tired.*
option_feedback: Being tired is not a rule; it is a logical conclusion.

questions.question: What does the modal in bold express? *You **should** apologise to her.*
option_feedback: It tells you to do something, not to avoid it.
It is not about being able to.

questions.question: What does the modal in bold express? *You **needn't** wear a tie on Saturdays.*
option_feedback: It is not forbidden; it is just not required.
It is about requirement, not ability.

questions.question: What does the modal in bold express? ***Shall** we start the meeting now?*
option_feedback: It does not ask whether it is compulsory.
It is a question that proposes an idea.

questions.question: State whether the following statement is true or false: Modals take -s with *he, she* and *it*.
questions.explanation: Modals never change: *he can, she must, it may*.
option_feedback: Not quite. Modals never change: *he can, she must, it may*.
Correct! Modals never change: *he can, she must, it may*.

questions.question: State whether the following statement is true or false: *mustn't* and *needn't* mean the same thing.
questions.explanation: *mustn't* = it is not allowed; *needn't* = it is not necessary.
option_feedback: Not quite. *mustn't* = it is not allowed; *needn't* = it is not necessary.
Correct! *mustn't* = it is not allowed; *needn't* = it is not necessary.

questions.question: State whether the following statement is true or false: *should have* + V3 shows that something right was not done in the past.
questions.explanation: *You should have called* = you did not call, and that was wrong.
option_feedback: Correct! *You should have called* = you did not call, and that was wrong.
Not quite. *You should have called* = you did not call, and that was wrong.

questions.question: State whether the following statement is true or false: *ought* is always followed by *to*.
option_feedback: Correct! *We ought to help the poor.*
Not quite. *We ought to help the poor.*

questions.question: State whether the following statement is true or false: The opposite of *He must be at home* (deduction) is *He mustn't be at home*.
questions.explanation: For deduction, the opposite of *must* is *can't*: *He can't be at home*.
option_feedback: Not quite. For deduction, the opposite of *must* is *can't*: *He can't be at home*.
Correct! For deduction, the opposite of *must* is *can't*: *He can't be at home*.

questions.question: State whether the following statement is true or false: *be able to* can be used where *can* has no form, such as the future: *will be able to*.
questions.explanation: *can* has no future or perfect forms, so we use *be able to*.
option_feedback: Correct! *can* has no future or perfect forms, so we use *be able to*.
Not quite. *can* has no future or perfect forms, so we use *be able to*.
